overview.text: Unemployment describes a situation in which people in the labor force do not have jobs. In U.S. official statistics, a person generally counts as unemployed if they are not working, are available for work, and actively searched during the previous four weeks; an exception applies to people temporarily laid off and expecting recall. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the labor force, not the whole population. Economists distinguish frictional unemployment, as people take time to move between jobs; structural unemployment, when workers’ skills or locations do not match available jobs; and cyclical unemployment, which rises when a recession reduces hiring. Frictional and structural unemployment can persist even in a healthy economy, so unemployment is not automatically zero.

key_facts.text: The labor force consists of employed and unemployed people; the official unemployment rate divides the unemployed by the labor force.

Under the U.S. Current Population Survey definition, unemployed people are generally jobless, available for work, and actively searching; people on temporary layoff who expect recall are an exception.
People who have stopped actively searching—including discouraged workers—are not counted as unemployed in the official U.S. measure.
Frictional unemployment occurs while people enter the job market or transition between jobs.
Structural unemployment results from a mismatch between workers’ skills or location and the jobs available.
Cyclical unemployment is linked to the business cycle: it tends to rise in recessions and fall during expansions.
